common_name: Niedersachsen Hydrangea (Lower Saxony German Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in spring after the last frost or in early fall, choosing a site with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the large flower heads from wilting in summer heat.

directions: This vigorous 1913 German introduction from breeder Wintergalen produces rounded mophead trusses that shift readily between lavender-blue and clear pink depending on soil acidity. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture, since the heavy flower clusters can flop in full afternoon sun. Prune only lightly in late winter, removing dead wood and spent stems just above a healthy bud, since flowers form on old wood. Mulch the root zone to buffer soil temperature swings and extend bloom into late summer.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant in spring once frost danger has passed, spacing generously since the sparse branching habit needs room for the oversized flower heads to display without crowding.

directions: Introduced in 1923, this old European cultivar is prized for mophead trusses that can reach nearly nine inches across on relatively few, widely spaced stems. Stake young plants in windy sites, since the sheer weight of the blooms can bow the branches before the wood thickens with age. Expect pale blue flowers in acidic soil or soft pink in neutral-to-alkaline soil, with color shifting most dramatically in containers. Deadhead spent trusses after bloom to tidy the plant, but avoid hard pruning, which sacrifices next year's old-wood flowers.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Königin Wilhelmina Hydrangea (Queen Wilhelmina Historic Dutch Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in spring in a bed with morning sun and afternoon shade, which helps preserve the unusual greenish-to-salmon-pink flower tones this cultivar is named for.

directions: Named for the Dutch monarch, this historic mophead opens a soft green that matures through violet tones into an unusual salmon-pink, a sequence that makes it a conversation piece among older hydrangea collections. The serrated sepal tips set it apart from smoother-edged mopheads at a glance. Keep soil evenly moist through summer, since drought stress shortens the color-change display considerably. Prune lightly after flowering, cutting only to a strong bud on stems that bloomed, to protect next season's old-wood buds.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Souvenir du Président Doumer Hydrangea (Historic French Deep Red-Purple Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in spring in reliably moist soil; this compact cultivar tolerates more sun than most mopheads as long as roots stay consistently damp.

directions: Bred in France in 1932 by Henri Cayeux and named for a French president, this tidy mophead carries dome-shaped trusses that run from deep rosy red in alkaline soil to rich purple or blue-tinged tones in acidic soil. Its naturally compact habit makes it a good fit for smaller borders where larger German cultivars would overwhelm the space. Water deeply during dry spells, since this selection shows wilting sooner than larger-leaved relatives. Light pruning right after bloom, removing only spent flower stems, keeps the rounded form tidy without reducing next year's flower count.

common_name: Domotoi Hydrangea (Antique Japanese Double-Flowered Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in spring in partial shade; the loose, irregular double flower heads hold their form longer out of direct afternoon sun.

directions: This antique Japanese selection, dating to the Edo period and also traded as 'Setsuka-yae', produces loosely doubled florets in irregular, almost ruffled clusters rather than a tight mophead dome. Flower color drifts from pale pink in neutral soil to a soft violet-blue-mauve in acidic conditions, with individual florets often showing both shades at once. Give it room to spread, since the vigorous, rounded habit fills out wider than many modern compact mopheads. Avoid late-season hard pruning, as the unusual double form blooms entirely on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant in spring in dappled shade to full sun with moist, humus-rich soil; mix with other hydrangeas in a border for a continuous summer-to-fall bloom display.

directions: Named for the German region, this cultivar produces enormous rounded mophead trusses from midsummer well into autumn, outlasting many earlier-blooming mopheads. Flower color follows soil chemistry in the usual way, shifting from blue in acidic ground to pink in alkaline ground. Its rounded, evenly proportioned habit makes it a reliable anchor plant in a mixed hydrangea border. Cut spent blooms back to a healthy bud after frost knocks the foliage down, leaving the rest of the stems untouched until late winter shaping.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Parzifal Hydrangea (Multi-Toned Pink-to-Purple German Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in spring with strong stems in mind; this upright grower tolerates slightly more sun than typical mopheads once established.

directions: This German-bred mophead is notable for carrying several shades of dark pink and dark purple within the same flower truss, rather than aging to a single uniform color. Sturdy, upright stems hold the lacy-textured flower heads well above the small, bright green foliage without flopping. Feed lightly in early spring and keep soil consistently moist through bud set to encourage the fullest color variation. Prune only immediately after flowering, removing spent stems back to a strong bud to protect the following year's old-wood blooms.
sources: Hydrangeas! A Guide for Gardeners, Horticulturists & Botanists (van Gelderen & van Gelderen)

common_name: Deutschland Hydrangea (Historic Dutch-Bred Pink-to-Red Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in spring in a bushy border setting with reliable moisture; despite its name this selection is actually a 1921 Dutch introduction, not German.

directions: Raised in 1921 by Dutch horticulturist D. Baardse, this century-old cultivar forms generously sized, flattened-ball mophead trusses on a bushy, vigorous shrub. Flowers run bright pink turning deep red in neutral soil, or shift toward mauve tones where soil is more acidic. Its long garden history and easy-growing nature have kept it in circulation among heritage hydrangea collectors long after flashier modern cultivars appeared. Water deeply during establishment and mulch well, since the broad, dense canopy can shade out its own root zone unevenly in its first two seasons.
sources: Hydrangeas! A Guide for Gardeners, Horticulturists & Botanists (van Gelderen & van Gelderen)
